name: Ben Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at an open-pit copper mine, and I'm one of the lead operators on the autonomous truck trial. Most days I'm still in a manned truck, hauling ore to the crusher, but two days a fortnight I'm with the trial crew. There I ride along, flag where the driverless trucks hesitate, and help the tech team set up the no-go zones. I'm on the newer pay deal for recent hires, so I earn less than the guys who started ten years ago doing the same work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being in the middle of something new. I use AI every day, for my study notes and to sort the trial data before I hand it to the engineers. What wears me out is the money, honestly. I put most of my savings into a drone and a pilot licence course, so I've got maybe two weeks in the bank, and I share a house with two other guys from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. So the trial trucks stay a gimmick. That would surprise me, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tech didn't live up to the sales pitch. At work I'd say let's keep the useful bits, like the collision alerts. Online I'd probably post a few of my trial videos and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit flat. I bet on being the guy who knows the new system, and in that world the new system doesn't matter much. I'd be back to just driving, on the lower pay deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and push through the union for recent hires to move onto the older pay deal. I'd start using the drone licence for weekend survey work on the farms around here, that's a few hundred dollars a job. And I'd keep using AI for the boring parts, like quotes and invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated. Not worried exactly, just itchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would hire a drone pilot out here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farmers mostly, for fence lines and dams after floods. The shire council sometimes needs road photos too. It's not a living, but it'd get me to a month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine for something more interesting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without something lined up. There's nothing else like it within three hours. I'm adventurous, but not stupid.

Do weekend **drone survey** work for local farms.
Use **AI** for drone quotes and invoices.

Use AI to write drone quotes and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is basically what I'm living. The trial goes well and they roll it out slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so you might as well be on the inside. At work I'd tell the younger drivers to put their names down for the trial crew. Online I'd keep posting what it's actually like, because people imagine it's worse or better than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. They'll need people who know the trucks and the system, at least for the rollout. The question is whether that job pays better than driving, and with this company I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the fleet controller role the minute it's advertised, the one watching the driverless trucks from the control room. I'd do the online automation course the truck maker offers, it's free for trial crews. And I'd keep the drone work going, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit worried about my mates who drive manned trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mates Craig and Ollie, who I started with. They're good drivers, but they hate the trial and won't sign up. I keep telling them the driverless trial is a lifeboat, not a betrayal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the controller job might not pay more. Would you take it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it lasts longer than driving. I'd rather earn the same in a job with a future. Then I'd argue about the pay once I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side. The fleet controller job is thinking work, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not something you can stop, so the government should help people move rather than try to hold it back. At work I'd tell people to get practical skills. Online I'd share what I know about the trucks, so people aren't scared of rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the control room job I wanted goes in 2028, because AI can watch the fleet better than me. The trucks were already driving themselves, so manned driving goes even sooner. What's left is the hands-on stuff for about three years, like fixing sensors and recovering bogged trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move straight into a field technician job with the truck maker, the people who install and fix the sensors on site. I'd move to wherever they send me, I've got no kids and no mortgage. I'd use AI to cram the electrical basics in the first six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but moving. I'd rather run than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two weeks of savings. Could you afford to move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they paid for the move, which these companies usually do for field techs. I'd sell the drone if I had to. I wouldn't go without a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when robots can do the hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble like everyone else. I'd hope by then I've saved something and know the systems well enough to manage them. But honestly, I don't know.

say: It can't be stopped, so government should help people **move** rather than hold it back.
I'd tell people at work to get **practical skills** fast.
think: The **control room** job goes in 2028, because AI watches the fleet better.

Use AI to **cram** electrical basics in six months.

fieldNote: He quickly sees that **thinking AI** removes the controller job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then three more. That's eight years of hands-on work, give or take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have time to get ready, but not to sit around. At work I'd push for a training budget for drivers. Online I'd keep posting about the trial, maybe more seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine for a while. I'd get into the control room, do it for a few years, then shift to the technician side before AGI in 2031. I'd basically be surfing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for fleet controller in the first year. Then I'd start an electrical certificate part time. I'd also save properly, a fixed amount every pay, because surfing it needs a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Energised, a bit wary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save each pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred a fortnight, which is a lot on my pay. I'd cut the takeaway and stop upgrading the drone. In two years that's about five grand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the drone work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but it'd be more about learning than money. Mapping a pit or a farm with a drone teaches you a lot about the software. That's what everything runs on.

say: There's time to **get ready**, but not to sit around.
The company should give drivers a **training budget** for the move.
think: I'd be **fine** for a while, moving from control room to technician.
do: Apply for **fleet controller** in the first year.
S3.quote: I'd get into the control room, do it for a few years, then shift to the technician side before AGI in 2031.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **plan two moves**, control room then technician.
He knows **surfing** the change needs savings.
Drone work becomes **learning** rather than money.

steps.text: Apply for the fleet controller role in the first year
Save two hundred dollars every fortnight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots three years after. That's practically my whole thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should use it to learn. At work I'd be the guy running lunchtime demos of the AI tools. Online I'd be pretty upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is good for me. I'd have time to get a proper qualification, maybe an engineering degree part time. The money's still tight now, but the long game looks fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the control room first. Then I'd start a part-time engineering degree online. I'd keep the drone business going and maybe grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit worried about the tight money for the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in this town for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not the whole time. Once I've got the degree, I'd go where the work is. But I'd stay while I study, rent's cheap here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone like Craig, who won't go near the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't push him. Some people are happy in a cab, and with ten years a driver can finish a career and retire into something else at forty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The control room job I'm aiming at goes almost as soon as I'd get it, and the hands-on work only lasts three more years. What would help is companies paying for the move into technician roles, and some way to save on a lower pay deal, like being moved onto the older one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people already working with the robots. We know where the driverless trucks get confused, what the tech team misses, and how drivers feel. Nobody asks us, they just ask the managers.

headlineQuote: We know where the driverless trucks get confused, what the tech team misses, and how drivers feel. Nobody asks us, they just ask the managers.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** haul truck lead operator on his copper mine's autonomous truck trial.
He uses **AI every day**, has about two weeks saved, and runs weekend drone surveys.
He is **pragmatic** and wants government to help people move, not stop the change.
In slower pictures he plans a **control room** job, then a technician or engineering path.
In AGI by 2028 he is **anxious**, betting on field technician work for three years.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because the control room job vanishes as soon as he gets it.
whatWouldHelp: Companies **paying for moves** into technician roles.
Being moved onto the **older pay deal** so he can save.
